summary: A 1977 note warning designers of Telnet options about a possible pitfall involving the Telnet sync sequence, which discards data until a data mark arrives. An option subnegotiation could be defined that would be lost this way.

plainLanguage.summary: If a clean-up crew throws away everything until a certain marker, an important message in between could be thrown out too. This note warns about that.

questions: telnet option design problem data mark
how does telnet sync affect options
subtitle: A warning about Telnet option interaction with the sync sequence.

tldr.problem: Telnet's sync sequence discards all data until a data mark arrives. If a Telnet option subnegotiation (like changing text display mode) arrives before that sync sequence, it could apply to the wrong data after recovery.
tldr.mechanism: The note identifies the interaction and proposes two solutions: either include affected data as part of the subnegotiation (non-standard) or define a recovery subnegotiation after the data mark to nullify unintended effects.
tldr.outcome: The warning helped inform future Telnet option design, though the specific scenario did not occur in deployed options.

today: RFC 728 is a historical design caution that has not been a significant problem in practice, as the interaction has been avoided in deployed Telnet options. It remains a useful reference for protocol designers about subtle interactions in protocol layering.

sections.title: The Sync Sequence Problem
sections.content: RFC 728 warns designers of Telnet options about a subtle interaction with the Telnet sync sequence. The sync sequence is a recovery mechanism that discards all data from the stream until a data mark is encountered, allowing a receiver to resynchronize after errors. Telnet control functions and option negotiation are not affected by the sync sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet has a way to clean up when things go wrong: it throws away data until it finds a special marker.

sections.title: The Interaction Pitfall
sections.content: A problem could arise if a future Telnet option subnegotiation affects the data that follows it in the stream (for example, instructing the terminal to display subsequent text in a special font or with special formatting). If a sync sequence is sent after such a subnegotiation but before that subnegotiation's intended data is processed, the subnegotiation's effect could be applied to the wrong data—the data that remains after the sync sequence discards everything up to the data mark.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a command to change the terminal to a special mode, then a clean-up sequence that throws away data. The mode change might affect the wrong text.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions
sections.content: Two solutions are identified. The first is to include the data to be affected as a parameter of the subnegotiation itself, before the subnegotiation ends. The disadvantage is that this violates Telnet design philosophy and would be confusing if a sync happened midway through—the user would see unexpected data loss and formatting changes. The second solution is for option designers to define a recovery subnegotiation that follows immediately after a data mark to nullify any effects of subnegotiations that were lost or misapplied. The exact mechanism would be specific to each option.
sections.plainLanguage: Either send the data to protect as part of the mode command itself, or define a way to undo accidental mode changes after recovery.

references.text: Postel, J., "Telnet Protocol Specification", RFC 764, June 1980.
